craft_claim: Irreverence is safe only inside a frame the audience recognizes as licensed — ritual, festival, genre convention, established persona — and breaches of that frame are policed as failed or offensive humor.

supporting_evidence.note: Joking relationships exist by social definition: insult is permitted because the relationship licenses it, and the license varies by pair and setting — permission is structural, not universal.
Carnival license is explicitly temporary and bounded in time and place — inversion is permitted because everyone knows when it ends.
Kyōgen occupies a sanctioned, fixed slot within the nō program and holds a bounded comic role (including restraint from mere slapstick) — comic insolence permitted because the program grants it.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole-book citation (open-access text read earlier in session)
supporting_evidence.note: The study of failed humor documents the policing side: when license or competence fails, audiences punish the attempt instead of laughing — the frame breach has social cost.

counterevidence.note: License conventions are culture-, platform-, and relationship-specific (visible in §E's variation across Japan, India, Anatolia, France) — there is no single universal license to invoke, only local ones to read correctly.

scope: All uses of the tone in someone else's space: publication, platform, ritual, genre, persona; the license must be legible to the specific audience before deflation begins.
exceptions: Writers with an established persona (the curmudgeon, the deadpan guide-voice) carry a portable license — but it was earned and can be revoked by misuse.
Where no license can be established, the voice must yield to plain or reverent register (card §4 restraint).
